messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a 25-year-old single man who works as a housekeeper in a downtown hotel, and when he first began to speak about his childhood, he did so haltingly, as if even putting words to it might pull him back inside it. He grew up with a caregiver who beat him behind closed doors, often at night, when the house was dark and the rest of the family was asleep. What stayed with him most was not only the violence itself but the whole sensory field around it: waking suddenly in darkness, hearing a younger child crying in another room and knowing no one was coming, feeling the rough texture of an old blanket and upholstered chair against his skin while he was pinned down and told to keep still. Even now, those details seem to hold the event in place for him more than any orderly narrative. He says the memories do not come back as something that happened long ago but “like a movie” that starts playing without his consent, so vivid across sound, touch, and bodily sensation that he has to stop talking when it happens because he is overwhelmed too fast.

Over time, Ethan came to believe that the world had taught him an irreversible lesson: you can never know who will harm you. He watches people closely for shifts in tone or movement, certain that danger is hidden inside ordinary encounters. He has also come to feel marked by what happened, as though other people can see it on him immediately, and beneath that is a more corrosive feeling that he is less like a person than an object that can be used or handled. Those beliefs sharpen what he notices. A child crying in the hallway of the hotel does not register to him as just noise; it lands with immediate force, as if it confirms that helplessness and threat are nearby again. Waking before dawn in a dark room feels charged before he has even fully opened his eyes. Certain scratchy cleaning fabrics and furniture textures catch his attention instantly, in a way he cannot dismiss.

At work these reactions have become woven into his routines. If he is assigned evening turnover or asked to clean a room with blackout curtains still drawn, he becomes intensely on guard, his heart racing and his body tightening before he has fully taken in why. When he hears children crying in adjoining rooms, or his hand brushes a rough bedspread that resembles what he remembers from childhood, the memory can ignite at once: the scene replaying, sensory and immediate, to the point that he momentarily feels he is back there rather than in a hotel room with a cart of linens. He describes brief episodes in which he freezes or loses track of where he is, followed by shaking, nausea, and a pounding chest. These reminders do not just bring back the memory; the memory itself seems to make the reminders spread, so that darkness, certain textures, and the sound of children have all become loaded and hard to escape in daily life.

Because of that, Ethan has built his life around preventing those moments. He tries never to be alone with another person, lingering where coworkers are visible or finding reasons to keep doors open while he cleans. He drops responsibilities when he thinks a task will put him at risk, leaving floors unfinished, trading away evening assignments, or calling out altogether if he knows he will wake in the dark and have to cross his apartment alone. He also disappears mentally, drifting into elaborate fantasy when he feels himself getting close to the edge, because it is the only way he knows to get some distance from what is coming up. In the short term these strategies feel necessary. If he walks away from a crying child in the hallway, keeps another housekeeper nearby, or lets his mind leave the room entirely, he may avoid the worst of the surge.

But the pattern has tightened around him. The more he organizes his day to escape reminders, the smaller and more precarious his world becomes, and the less chance he has to discover that the present is different from the past. When he leaves a task unfinished or mentally checks out, the memory remains unprocessed and returns later with the same force, replaying in full until he has to shut down the recall. He then takes his own evasions as evidence that he is damaged in some visible, essential way. Being unable to stay in a dark room or finish cleaning when a child is crying nearby makes him feel exposed, certain others can tell something is wrong with him just by looking at him. Needing to position himself so he is never alone with anyone reinforces his conviction that no person is truly safe. Even his drifting away leaves him ashamed afterward, more convinced he is absent, unreal, more object than man.

He finally sought help after a recent incident on the night shift. He was alone finishing a family suite when he heard a child crying in the corridor and, at the same moment, reached across a coarse upholstered bench. He suddenly felt the old scene take over completely. A coworker found him crouched by the bathroom door, sweating and unresponsive, and management later warned him about repeated incomplete assignments. Ethan came in frightened that he is losing control and will not be able to keep his job. What he fears most is that he will always live as if harm is about to happen again; what he hopes, more quietly, is that he might someday be in a dark room, hear ordinary sounds, feel ordinary things, and remain fully in the present.
